When the conversation grows long, some or all of the current context is summarized; the summary, along with any remaining unsummarized context, is provided in the next context window so work can continue — you don't need to wrap up early or hand off mid-task.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

# Marketing Plan: Handmade Candle Shop on Etsy

> Fill in the `[brackets]` with your shop's details. Review the plan every quarter.

## 1. Goals (First 6 Months)

| Metric | Target |
|---|---|
| Monthly orders | [e.g., 40 → 120] |
| Listing conversion rate | 2–4% |
| Repeat customer rate | 20%+ |
| Reviews | 50+ at 4.8★ or higher |
| Email subscribers | 300+ |
| Instagram/TikTok followers | [e.g., 1,000] |

## 2. Brand & Positioning

- **Shop name / tagline:** [ ]
- **What makes you different:** [e.g., soy wax, small batch, hand-poured, sustainable packaging, unique scent stories]
- **Brand voice:** warm, sensory, personal. Describe how a scent *feels*, not just what's in it.
- **Visual identity:** consistent palette, label design, and photo style across Etsy, social and packaging.

## 3. Target Customers

1. **Self-gifters / home decor lovers** (25–45): want cozy, aesthetic ambiance.
2. **Gift buyers**: birthdays, housewarming, teachers, weddings, Mother's Day, holidays.
3. **Corporate/event buyers**: bulk favors, client gifts, bridal parties.
4. **Wellness seekers**: aromatherapy, self-care, clean ingredients.

## 4. Etsy SEO (Highest-Leverage Channel)

**Listing titles:** lead with the phrase buyers search, e.g. "Soy Candle, Lavender Vanilla, Hand Poured Gift for Her".

**Tags (all 13 used):** mix long-tail phrases such as `soy wax candle`, `housewarming gift`, `scented candle gift`, `self care gift`, `cozy home decor`, `[scent] candle`.

**Attributes:** fill in all fields (scent, occasion, material, color).

**Descriptions:** put the key details in the first 160 characters, then include scent notes, burn time, wax and wick type, size, and safety info.

**Photos (use all 10 slots):**
1. Hero shot, clean and well lit
2. Lit, in a lifestyle setting
3. Scale shot with hand or object
4. Scent notes graphic
5. Packaging / gift-ready view
6. Close-up of texture and label
7. Collection / bundle shot
8. Burn time and care instructions
9. Customer photo or review
10. Short video (5–15 sec)

**Ongoing:** check Etsy Stats monthly. Refresh the titles and tags of weak listings. Renew or re-list seasonally.

## 5. Product & Pricing Strategy

- **Core line:** 3–5 signature scents, with two sizes each (e.g., 8 oz and 12 oz).
- **Entry item:** a mini or sample set ($8–12) to lower the risk of a first purchase.
- **Bundles:** trio sets, "build your own" boxes, and gift sets. These raise average order value.
- **Seasonal drops:** limited editions create urgency (see calendar below).
- **Pricing:** cost of materials + labor + Etsy fees (~6.5% transaction + payment processing + listing fee) + shipping goal + 30–50% margin. Don't underprice; candles at $5 signal low quality.
- **Free shipping threshold:** set slightly above your average order value (e.g., free over $35) to encourage add-ons.

## 6. Etsy Tools

- **Etsy Ads:** start at $1–3/day on your 2–3 best-converting listings. Review after 30 days; keep only listings with a positive return.
- **Sales & discounts:** use for holidays, "first order" coupons, and abandoned-cart offers. Offers to people who favorited an item often convert well.
- **Etsy's "Star Seller" targets:** respond to messages within 24 hours, ship on time, and keep reviews high. Star Seller status improves visibility.
- **Reviews:** include a thank-you card asking for an honest review. Reply to every review.

Pick **two** platforms and do them well.

| Platform | Content | Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| **Instagram** (Reels + Stories) | Pouring process, lit-candle ambiance, scent stories, packing orders | 3–4 posts/week |
| **TikTok** | "Day in the life of a candle maker," ASMR pours, small-business packing videos | 3–5 videos/week |
| **Pinterest** | Pins linking to listings (cozy decor, gift guides). Slow burn, but long-lived traffic | 5–10 pins/week |

1. Behind the scenes (making, testing, sourcing)
2. Lifestyle/aesthetic (candles in rooms, seasonal styling)
3. Education (candle care, wick trimming, why soy wax)
4. Social proof (reviews, customer photos)
5. Offers & launches

**Tips:** link to Etsy directly in bio (or use a link hub); use a consistent set of hashtags (`#handmadecandles #soycandles #smallbusiness #etsyshop`); reply to every comment.

Etsy doesn't hand you customer emails to market to, so build your own list.

- Put a **QR code or card** in each package: "Get 10% off your next order + early access to new scents."

- **Cadence:** 2 emails/month — new releases, restock alerts, seasonal gift guides.
- **Etsy-side retention:** offer a coupon to past buyers through Etsy's built-in marketing tools; follow up with a thank-you message after delivery.

Packaging is marketing.

- A free sample (mini candle or wax melt) for repeat or large orders.
- Make it photo-worthy to encourage customers to share it.
- Include social handles and the email-signup QR code.

## 10. Seasonal Calendar

| Month | Focus |
|---|---|
| Jan | "New year, self-care" scents; clearance of holiday stock |
| Feb | Valentine's gifts (start promoting early January) |
| Mar–Apr | Spring florals, Easter, Mother's Day pre-launch |
| May | Mother's Day, teacher appreciation, wedding season |
| Jun–Jul | Light, fresh scents; Father's Day; summer sale |
| Aug–Sep | Back-to-school; fall scents debut early |
| Oct | Halloween, autumn bestsellers |
| **Nov–Dec** | **Biggest season.** Gift sets, Black Friday/Cyber Monday, shipping cutoff reminders. Stock up by September. |

- **Local:** farmers markets, craft fairs, boutique wholesale or consignment (also a good way to get photos and testimonials).
- **Collaborations:** pair with a tea maker, soap maker, or bookshop for cross-promotion.
- **Gift guides & press:** pitch bloggers and local media for holiday gift roundups.
- **Corporate/wedding favors:** add a listing for bulk and custom-label orders.

## 12. Safety & Trust

Customers (and Etsy) expect: warning labels, burn-time guidance, wick-trimming instructions, and compliant labeling for your region (e.g., CPSC guidelines in the US). Mention these on your listings and in your care card.

**Days 1–30: Foundation**
- [ ] Audit every listing: title, 13 tags, attributes, 10 photos, video
- [ ] Reshoot hero photos with consistent style
- [ ] Add a mini/sample set and 2 bundles
- [ ] Create package inserts with email QR code
- [ ] Set up email tool and social accounts

**Days 31–60: Traction**
- [ ] Post on social 3–4×/week; start Pinterest pins
- [ ] Run Etsy Ads on top 2–3 listings
- [ ] Reach out to 10 micro-influencers
- [ ] Launch first limited-edition seasonal scent
- [ ] Ask every buyer for a review

**Days 61–90: Optimize & Scale**
- [ ] Review stats: top traffic sources, conversion, best sellers
- [ ] Double down on what works; drop what doesn't
- [ ] Send first email campaign
- [ ] Apply to 1–2 local markets or wholesale accounts
- [ ] Plan next quarter's seasonal line

## 14. Budget (Example, Monthly)

| Item | Cost |
|---|---|
| Etsy Ads | $30–90 |
| Photo props / lighting | $20–40 |
| Packaging inserts & stickers | $30–60 |
| Email platform | $0–20 |
| Influencer samples | $30–60 |
| Market/fair fees (occasional) | $0–75 |
| **Total** | **~$110–350** |

## 15. Metrics to Track (Monthly)

- Etsy: visits, conversion rate, favorites, revenue, top listings, search terms
- Ads: spend, revenue, ROAS (aim for at least 2–3×)
- Social: reach, engagement, link clicks
- Email: subscribers, open rate, click rate
- Business: average order value, repeat-customer rate, profit margin

**Rule of thumb:** if a listing gets views but no sales, fix photos and price. If it gets no views, fix SEO. If it sells well, promote it.

That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).

    DIMENSIONS,

    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

# Part 2: Going Deeper

## 16. Unit Economics (Know Your Numbers First)

Work this out per product before spending on ads. Example for a 8 oz candle priced at $28:

| Line | Amount |
|---|---|
| Wax, fragrance, wick, jar, label | $6.50 |
| Packaging (box, tissue, insert) | $1.80 |
| Labor (20 min at $18/hr) | $6.00 |
| Etsy fees (~6.5% + ~3% + $0.25 processing + $0.20 listing) | ~$2.20 |
| Offsite Ads fee, if it applies (12–15%) | $0–4.20 |
| **Total cost** | **~$16.50–20.70** |
| **Profit** | **~$7.30–11.50 (26–41%)** |

**Why it matters:**
- **Break-even ROAS** = price ÷ profit. At $9 profit on $28, break-even ROAS is about 3.1×. Ads below that lose money on first purchase.
- **Max customer acquisition cost** = profit on first order + expected profit from repeats. If 20% reorder twice, you can afford a bit more than $9 per customer.
- **Shipping:** don't absorb it blindly. Build it into price, then offer "free shipping" as a framing.
- **Offsite Ads:** if you earn over $10k/yr you can't opt out and the fee drops to 12%. Under that, consider opting out if margins are thin, or price in the fee.

Create a simple spreadsheet with one row per SKU: cost, price, margin, break-even ROAS, units sold.

## 17. Keyword Research Process

1. **Seed list:** type each product idea into Etsy's search bar and note every autocomplete suggestion.
2. **Competitor scan:** open the top 10 results for your 5 best terms. Note their titles, tags, price, photo style, review count.
3. **Tools:** eRank, Marmalead, or Alura (free tiers work to start) for search volume vs. competition.
4. **Score each phrase:** high demand, low competition, and relevant to *your* product beats a broad term like "candle."
5. **Group by intent:**
   - *Product:* soy candle, amber jar candle, wooden wick candle
   - *Scent:* lavender vanilla candle, cedar and smoke, fig candle
   - *Occasion/gift:* housewarming gift, teacher gift, bridesmaid gift, sympathy gift
   - *Style/aesthetic:* cottagecore, minimalist, boho, dark academia
   - *Benefit:* relaxing, self care, aromatherapy, spa gift
6. **Assign** one primary phrase per listing. Avoid making your own listings compete with each other.

**Example title formula:**
`[Primary phrase] | [Scent] | [Material/size] | [Gift angle]`
→ `Lavender Vanilla Soy Candle | Hand Poured 8oz Wooden Wick | Relaxing Self Care Gift for Her`

## 18. Listing Copy Template

```
[Opening line: the feeling, e.g., "Quiet evenings, soft light, and the scent of lavender fields after rain."]

SCENT NOTES
Top: ... | Heart: ... | Base: ...

DETAILS
• 8 oz / 226 g, approx. 45 hr burn time
• 100% natural soy wax, cotton/wooden wick
• Phthalate-free fragrance oil
• Hand poured in small batches in [location]

PERFECT FOR
Housewarming, birthdays, thank-yous, treating yourself

CARE & SAFETY
Trim wick to 1/4". Burn 2–3 hours at a time. Never leave unattended. Keep away from children and pets.

SHIPPING
Ships in X days in a protective, gift-ready box. [Add gift note option]

[Closing line + invite: "Message me for custom scents or bulk orders."]
```

Add an **FAQ** (burn time, vegan, pet safety, custom labels, returns) to cut pre-sale messages.

## 19. Etsy Ads Playbook

- **Phase 1 (weeks 1–4):** $2/day on 2 listings with the best conversion rate and good reviews. Don't judge before about 100 clicks.
- **Phase 2:** if ROAS is above break-even (see §16), raise budget by about 20% every week, and add 1 new listing at a time.
- **Phase 3:** pause listings with 50+ clicks and no sales; fix the listing (photos, price, title) before re-enabling.
- **Seasonal:** raise budget 3–4 weeks before peak events (Mother's Day, Black Friday, Christmas) and lower it afterward.
- **Check:** only count sales attributed to ads, and compare against your organic baseline.

## 20. Product Launch Playbook (Per New Scent)

| When | Action |
|---|---|
| T-4 weeks | Test pour, burn test, get feedback from 5–10 people |
| T-3 weeks | Photograph; write the scent story and name |
| T-2 weeks | Tease on social ("guess the scent"); email subscribers a sneak peek |
| T-1 week | Open waitlist or pre-order with a small discount for subscribers |
| Launch day | List on Etsy; post Reels/TikTok; send email; share to Pinterest; update "New" section |
| T+1 week | Follow up with reviews; share customer reactions |
| T+4 weeks | Evaluate: units sold, conversion, repeat orders. Keep, tweak or retire |

**Limited editions:** cap quantity and say so ("only 60 made"). Scarcity is real, so keep it honest.

## 21. 12-Week Content Calendar Template

Repeat this weekly structure:

| Day | Content |
|---|---|
| Mon | Behind the scenes: pouring or testing a batch |
| Tue | Educational: candle care tip, wax comparison, wick trimming |
| Wed | Product spotlight: one scent with its story |
| Thu | Customer review / photo (with permission) |
| Fri | Aesthetic Reel: lit candle, cozy mood, trending audio |
| Sat | Packing orders / unboxing / shop life |
| Sun | Rest, or engage with comments and DMs |

**Video hooks that tend to work:**
- "Making 50 candles for my Etsy shop orders"
- "Why your candle tunnels (and how to fix it)"
- "Packing a $30 candle order, small business edition"
- "3 scents for your cozy autumn"
- "Soy vs. coconut vs. beeswax"

Batch-film once a week (2 hours), then schedule posts with Meta Business Suite or Later.

## 22. Email Automations (Set Up Once)

1. **Welcome series (3 emails):** (1) discount code + your story, (2) bestsellers + candle care tips, (3) social proof and reviews.
2. **Post-purchase:** thank-you with care instructions; day 10 ask for a review; day 30 suggest a complementary scent.
3. **Win-back (90 days):** "We miss you" with a small incentive.
4. **Restock/back-in-stock** alert for sold-out items.
5. **Seasonal campaigns:** gift guide 6 weeks before holidays; last-order-date reminder.

**Subject-line ideas:** "Your new favorite scent is here", "5 candles for a cozy weekend", "Last call: ships in time for Christmas".

## 23. Customer Acquisition by Segment

| Segment | Where to find them | Offer |
|---|---|---|
| Gift buyers | Etsy search, Pinterest gift guides | Gift-ready packaging, note option, bundles |
| Self-care buyers | Instagram/TikTok wellness niches | Relaxation scents, subscription box |
| Wedding/events | Etsy searches "wedding favors", Facebook groups | Custom labels, bulk pricing from 20+ |
| Corporate | LinkedIn, local business groups | Branded candles, net-30 invoicing, minimum 25 |
| Local | Markets, boutiques | Wholesale at 50% of retail, display kit |

## 24. Subscription & Repeat-Revenue Ideas

- **Candle of the Month** (via Etsy variations or an off-Etsy store): lower the price slightly for commitment.
- **Refill program:** return jars for a discount (sustainability angle).
- **Loyalty card:** buy 5, get a mini free (include in packaging).
- **Scent quiz** on your site/social to guide purchases and capture emails.

## 25. Reputation & Reviews System

- Insert a card: "Loved it? A review helps a small shop more than you know."
- Respond to *all* reviews in 24–48 hours; never argue publicly.
- For issues: reply fast, offer a replacement or refund, and keep the tone warm. A solved problem often becomes a good review.
- Feature the best quotes in listing photos and social posts.

## 26. Competitive Positioning Worksheet

For 5 competing shops, record:

| Shop | Price | Review count | Best-seller | Photo style | Weakness | Your opening |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | | | | | | |

Look for gaps: an under-served scent family, a missing size, weak photography, slow shipping, or no gift options. Then own one clear niche (e.g., "literary-inspired candles" or "non-toxic candles for sensitive noses") rather than competing on generic ones.

## 27. Experiments to Run (One at a Time)

| # | Test | How to measure | Duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | New hero photo vs. old | Conversion rate | 3–4 weeks |
| 2 | Price $28 vs. $32 | Orders and profit per view | 4 weeks |
| 3 | Free-shipping threshold $35 vs. $45 | Average order value | 4 weeks |
| 4 | Title rewrite | Impressions and click-through | 3 weeks |
| 5 | Add video to listing | Conversion rate | 3 weeks |
| 6 | Gift-note option on/off | Gift-segment sales | 4 weeks |

Change **one variable at a time**, and log the result in a spreadsheet. Etsy data is noisy, so wait for enough views (500+) before deciding.

## 28. Risks & Mitigations

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Overdependence on Etsy | Build email list, own site (Shopify/Squarespace) by month 6 |
| Seasonal cash crunch | Pre-buy materials with Q3 profits; offer pre-orders |

- **Visual identity:** consistent palette, label design, and photo style across Etsy, social and packaging.

## 3. Target Customers

1. **Self-gifters / home decor lovers** (25–45): want cozy, aesthetic ambiance.
2. **Gift buyers**: birthdays, housewarming, teachers, weddings, Mother's Day, holidays.
3. **Corporate/event buyers**: bulk favors, client gifts, bridal parties.
4. **Wellness seekers**: aromatherapy, self-care, clean ingredients.

## 4. Etsy SEO (Highest-Leverage Channel)

**Listing titles:** lead with the phrase buyers search, e.g. "Soy Candle, Lavender Vanilla, Hand Poured Gift for Her".

**Tags (all 13 used):** mix long-tail phrases such as `soy wax candle`, `housewarming gift`, `scented candle gift`, `self care gift`, `cozy home decor`, `[scent] candle`.

**Attributes:** fill in all fields (scent, occasion, material, color).

**Descriptions:** put the key details in the first 160 characters, then include scent notes, burn time, wax and wick type, size, and safety info.

1. Hero shot, clean and well lit
2. Lit, in a lifestyle setting
3. Scale shot with hand or object
4. Scent notes graphic
5. Packaging / gift-ready view
6. Close-up of texture and label
7. Collection / bundle shot
8. Burn time and care instructions
9. Customer photo or review
10. Short video (5–15 sec)

**Ongoing:** check Etsy Stats monthly. Refresh the titles and tags of weak listings. Renew or re-list seasonally.

## 5. Product & Pricing Strategy

- **Core line:** 3–5 signature scents, with two sizes each (e.g., 8 oz and 12 oz).
- **Entry item:** a mini or sample set ($8–12) to lower the risk of a first purchase.
- **Bundles:** trio sets, "build your own" boxes, and gift sets. These raise average order value.
- **Seasonal drops:** limited editions create urgency (see calendar below).
- **Pricing:** cost of materials + labor + Etsy fees (~6.5% transaction + payment processing + listing fee) + shipping goal + 30–50% margin. Don't underprice; candles at $5 signal low quality.
- **Free shipping threshold:** set slightly above your average order value (e.g., free over $35) to encourage add-ons.

## 6. Etsy Tools

- **Etsy Ads:** start at $1–3/day on your 2–3 best-converting listings. Review after 30 days; keep only listings with a positive return.
- **Sales & discounts:** use for holidays, "first order" coupons, and abandoned-cart offers. Offers to people who favorited an item often convert well.
- **Etsy's "Star Seller" targets:** respond to messages within 24 hours, ship on time, and keep reviews high. Star Seller status improves visibility.
- **Reviews:** include a thank-you card asking for an honest review. Reply to every review.

## 7. Social Media

Pick **two** platforms and do them well.

| Platform | Content | Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| **Instagram** (Reels + Stories) | Pouring process, lit-candle ambiance, scent stories, packing orders | 3–4 posts/week |
| **TikTok** | "Day in the life of a candle maker," ASMR pours, small-business packing videos | 3–5 videos/week |
| **Pinterest** | Pins linking to listings (cozy decor, gift guides). Slow burn, but long-lived traffic | 5–10 pins/week |

**Content pillars:**
1. Behind the scenes (making, testing, sourcing)
2. Lifestyle/aesthetic (candles in rooms, seasonal styling)
3. Education (candle care, wick trimming, why soy wax)
4. Social proof (reviews, customer photos)
5. Offers & launches

## 8. Email & Customer Retention

Etsy doesn't hand you customer emails to market to, so build your own list.

- Put a **QR code or card** in each package: "Get 10% off your next order + early access to new scents."
